title: Recovery strategies

draft.title: Recovery strategies
card: Training puts stress on the body. Recovery strategies help it repair and adapt between sessions, so an athlete can train well again.
Most repair happens during sleep, so too little sleep can slow recovery. Active recovery is light, low-intensity movement after hard exercise, such as an easy walk or swim.
Using water to aid recovery, such as cold water immersion or a contrast bath that switches between cold and warm. Massage works the muscles by hand to ease soreness and tightness.
Eating and drinking after training supplies carbohydrate to refuel muscles, protein to repair them, and fluid to replace what was lost in sweat.
draft.remember: Recovery is when the body repairs and adapts, and each strategy supports that repair.

a.q: Which choice is an example of active recovery?
opts: An easy 20-minute swim the day after a hard match
A full rest day spent lying on the couch
A cold bath straight after a training session
A protein shake eaten after a gym session
a.why: Active recovery is light, low-intensity movement, so an easy swim fits. A cold bath is hydrotherapy and a protein shake is nutrition. A rest day involves no movement, so it is not active recovery.
a.clue: Active means the athlete is still moving, but gently.

b.q: After a hard Saturday game, Jess, a netballer, sits in cold water for ten minutes and then drinks a recovery shake. Which two strategies is she using?
b.why: Sitting in cold water is hydrotherapy, and the shake supplies nutrients, so it is nutrition. Hydrotherapy is a tempting pairing with active recovery, but Jess is sitting still, so she is not doing light movement.
b.clue: Match the water and the drink to a strategy each.

a.best: An easy 20-minute swim the day after a hard match
